text: The Spanish didn't come to trade. They came to take — and they built an entire machine to do it. Paperwork and whips, priests and ledgers, all pointed at one goal: extraction. You're watching APUSH Explained. Let's get into it.

Last video: why Europe sailed. This video: what Spain built when it arrived. [pause:0.45] Here's the setup. By 1521 Tenochtitlan has fallen; by 1532 Pizarro has taken the Inca. A few hundred Spaniards now rule millions of Native people. How? Not with guns — with paper. The Spanish crown ran its empire like a law firm with an army attached. Every theft had a document. Every document had a seal. The point is: the conquest wasn't chaos. It was administration.

First arm of the machine: the encomienda. Here's the legal fiction. The crown grants a Spaniard — an encomendero — the right to collect tribute and labor from a group of Native people. In exchange, he's supposed to protect them and teach them Christianity. [pause:0.45] Supposed to. In practice, it's forced labor with a cross on top.

And here's the thesis of this whole video — say it with me: the encomienda was about labor, not land. Spain didn't want Native territory for farming. It wanted Native bodies for working. [TIP]Remember this: encomienda equals labor, not land.[/TIP] Every exam question about the system turns on that distinction.
The paperwork even had a script for conquest itself. Before attacking a village, the Spanish were legally required to read the Requerimiento — the Requirement. Listen to the voice of the crown:

quote.source: El Requerimiento, written by Juan López de Palacios Rubios

text: “I certify to you that, with the help of God, we shall powerfully enter into your country, and shall make war against you in all ways and manners that we can.”
Read in Spanish. To people who spoke no Spanish. [pause:0.75] Then the attack was legal. The point is: the machine didn't hide its violence — it filed it.

Second arm: silver. In 1545 the Spanish find Potosí — a mountain of silver in the Andes so rich it bankrupts the metaphor. They work it with the mita, a draft-labor system that pulls Native men from hundreds of miles away. [pause:0.45] The silver flows to Spain, and Spain spends it across Europe and Asia — the first truly global currency. Prices rise everywhere. The point is: a mountain in Bolivia rewired the world's economy. Labor in, silver out — that's the machine's engine room.

Not everyone in Spain was comfortable with the machine. Bartolomé de las Casas, a friar who watched the conquest up close, wrote the empire's most devastating review — in Spanish, so the king couldn't miss it:

quote.source: Bartolomé de las Casas, Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias

text: “La causa porque han muerto y destruído tantas y tales e tan infinito número de ánimas los cristianos ha sido solamente por tener por su fin último el oro y henchirse de riquezas en muy breves días.”

The cause of so many deaths, he says: the Christians' ultimate end was gold. [pause:0.45] Las Casas helped win the New Laws of 1542 against Native enslavement — and the colonists mostly ignored them. The machine was bigger than its critics.

Third arm: hierarchy. As Spanish, Native, and African peoples had children together, the colony needed a filing system for human beings. The answer: the casta system — sixteen painted panels ranking every possible mixture. [pause:0.45] Look at the panels. Each one is a little family portrait with a label, like a field guide to people. The point is: race in Spanish America wasn't just prejudice — it was bureaucracy. Your caste decided your taxes, your job, who you could marry.

Read the label on this panel: “De español e india, mestiza.” From a Spaniard and an Indian woman, a mestiza child. [pause:0.45] That's it — a whole human identity, filed in five words. The Spanish invented race as paperwork, and the paperwork outlived the empire. When you see racial hierarchy on the exam, trace it here — this is where the filing system started.

So the point is this. The Spanish machine had three arms: forced labor dressed as law, silver dug by drafted hands, and a racial filing system painted in sixteen panels. [pause:0.75] Encomienda, Potosí, casta — labor, wealth, hierarchy. And when Native labor ran out — dead or fled — the machine switched fuels: enslaved Africans, shipped in under the asiento. The conquest gets the glory in the stories. The paperwork did the work.

That's the Spanish machine — labor, silver, hierarchy, all filed in triplicate. Next: the argument over whether any of it was right — Las Casas versus Sepúlveda at Valladolid, the debate that put conquest itself on trial. That's vid-u1-05, plus the drill set. Drill it, own it — I'll see you in the next one.
